taxes.reasoning: Split: profit tax is taken unchanged from companies_all.json; other taxes (VAT, excise, payroll, property, customs, exit taxes) = all taxes minus profit tax. The range of other taxes combines the ranges of all taxes and profit tax with correlation 0.6 (the all-tax estimate is half built on profit-tax shares), log-normal, at least +-10%. Owner measure (profit + half of other) totals are given under split_totals. Other taxes are 69-79% of all taxes (79% in 2021), so the owner measure is 60-66% of all taxes. Cross-check with FDI income: Bank of Russia direct investment income payable (after tax) grossed up at 20% (25% in 2025) implies profit tax of foreign direct investors of EUR 20.2bn (2021), 13.1, 8.7, 6.0 and 5.3bn (2022-2025). KSE in-scope profit tax is 23% of that in 2021 (the rest is round-trip capital via Cyprus and others and resource joint ventures) and 43-72% in 2022-2025; it never exceeds it. FDI income cannot be split by home country: the Bank of Russia stopped country data in 2022 and immediate-investor data are dominated by conduits. History 2018-2020: no tax series by home country exists before 2021 (KSE and B4Ukraine start in 2021; Rosstat publishes no FDI income by investor country). Each country's 2021 profit tax and other taxes are carried back with global indices in nominal EUR: profit tax with the geometric mean of the direct-investment-income ratio (2018 0.62, 2019 0.78, 2020 0.58 of 2021) and the Russian GDP in EUR ratio (0.91, 0.98, 0.85); low = income ratio x0.9, high = GDP ratio x1.1. Other taxes (turnover and payroll based) with the GDP-in-EUR ratio (low x0.9, high x1.08). A country factor moves each country by half its IMF DIP position change relative to all countries (Russia-reported and counterpart data, capped 0.75-1.33); conduits use the global index only. Ranges combine the 2021 range, the index range and the country factor (log-normal). Totals: 2018 EUR 18.2bn, 2019 20.8bn, 2020 17.6bn of all taxes (2021: 21.9bn); profit tax 3.3, 4.0, 3.2bn (2021: 4.6bn). The 2018-2021 average of all taxes is about 0.90 of 2021 and of profit tax about 0.83 of 2021.

china_refining.unit: EUR bn of Russian crude value (CREA delivered value); 2026 = Jan-Aug; calendar years (2022 includes Jan-Feb, as for Turkey and India)
china_refining.recommendation: deduct exported_crude_value from China's payments to Russia like Turkey and India (refiners block); add nothing at buyers

sources.name: UN Comtrade, China HS 2710 exports by partner 2022-2025 and HS 2709 imports
CREA Russia Fossil Tracker: Russian seaborne and pipeline crude to China, tonnes and EUR, 2022-Aug 2026
China customs via press: Jan-Aug 2026 refined product exports 34.24 Mt (-9.6% y/y); August 6.01 Mt; export quotas by company
Reuters via Hydrocarbon Processing: China eases controls on fuel exports for a second month (quota holders: state refiners and Zhejiang Petrochemical)

china_refining.reasoning: Exported Russian crude = China's refined product exports (HS 2710, UN Comtrade tonnes: 53.7, 62.7, 58.1, 58.0 Mt; 2026 Jan-Aug 34.2 Mt from customs via press, range 30-36 Mt because product scopes differ) x Russian share of refinery runs (CREA Russian crude incl. pipeline 87.8, 107.0, 108.5, 100.7, 77.5 Mt / NBS crude runs 676, 735, 708, about 738 and about 463 Mt = 13.0-16.7%) x an exporter factor 0.75 (0.45-1.10): export quotas are held by Sinopec, PetroChina, CNOOC, Sinochem and Zhejiang Petrochemical, while Shandong independents without product export quotas take a large part of seaborne Russian crude and Xinjiang/inland refineries take Kazakh-route pipeline crude / 0.93 t product per t crude (0.90-0.96) x CREA Russian crude value per tonne delivered to China. Result: EUR 3.3bn (2022), 3.6 (2023), 3.6 (2024), 2.7 (2025), 2.2 (2026 Jan-Aug), central; ranges about -45%/+65%. Already counted: the China component of energy.json laundered_oil (China HS 2710 exports to each buyer x Russian share of China's crude imports 17-20% x CREA calibration 0.53/0.699/1.0) is net of ship-registry destinations (Liberia, Panama, Marshall Islands etc., 12-16% of the value), which the GDP cap removes. It equals or exceeds the product value made from Russian crude in every year, because the model uses the import share (17-20%) rather than the run share (13-17%) and no exporter discount. So 98-100% is already counted at buyers (low end 0.37-0.53 when calibration is low and the export factor high); nothing new should be added to buyers. As for Turkey and India, the exported crude value is counted twice: in China's own payments to Russia and at the buyers. To match the refiners block, deduct exported_crude_value from China's payments (central from years, high from years_lo, low from years_hi). A side finding: the China component in laundered_oil (product value 3.8-4.9bn central) is 0.9-1.2x the product value we estimate was actually made from Russian crude (3.0-4.9bn), so it is not too low.

sources.name: CREA Russia Fossil Tracker: Russian crude (seaborne, pipeline, rail) to EU members 2021-Aug 2026

Eurostat energy balances (nrg_bal_c): refinery output and product exports by member state, used for export shares
Laundered oil model refiner set (IND, TUR, CHN, ARE)

eu_refiners.reasoning: The laundered-oil model (energy.json) has only four refiner countries: India, Turkey, China and the UAE. Fuel refined from Russian crude in EU refineries (Schwedt, Leuna, ISAB Priolo, Rotterdam/Zeeland, Plock/Gdansk, Neftochim Burgas, Slovnaft, MOL Danube, Litvinov/Kralupy, Petrotel and others) and sold to other countries is therefore NOT counted as laundered oil at any buyer. There is no double count, and no deduction is needed: the EU refiner country carries the full crude value in its own payments to Russia, including the part it exported. Size of the exported part (Russian crude value x refinery product export share, Eurostat-type balances, educated ranges): about EUR 21bn in 2022 (15.6-26.9), mostly Netherlands 5.9, Italy 4.8 (ISAB), Slovakia 1.9, Germany 1.6, Poland 1.6, Bulgaria 1.4, Hungary 0.9; then 3.4bn (2023), 2.1 (2024), 1.9 (2025), 0.8 (2026 Jan-Aug) from the Druzhba and Bulgarian exemptions (Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria 2023). Most of it went to other EU members and Switzerland; Ukraine also bought diesel from Slovnaft, MOL, Orlen and Neftochim (allowed under the embargo exemptions). If the map wanted the same treatment as Turkey and India, this would move from the refiner country to its buyers; we recommend leaving it with the refiner, because (a) in 2022 most of it is before the embargo and intra-EU, (b) no buyer split by crude origin exists, and (c) for 2023-2026 the derogations limited exports (Bulgaria banned exports of products from Russian crude except to Ukraine; Slovakia's permission to export them to Czechia was time-limited).

laundered_prewar_meta.unit: EUR bn product value per year, same stage as energy.json laundered_oil

sources.name: UN Comtrade: HS 2710 exports by partner of China, India, Turkey, UAE, 2018-2021; HS 2709 imports of China and India by partner
UN Comtrade: Russia-reported HS 2709 and 2710 exports to China, India, Turkey, UAE, 2018-2021
CREA Russia Fossil Tracker, 2021 crude and products to Turkey and UAE
CREA refining-loophole calibration factors

laundered_prewar_meta.reasoning: Same formula as the post-war model (CREA refining-loophole approach as implemented in energy.json): for each refiner (China, India, Turkey, UAE), HS 2710 exports to each buyer (UN Comtrade, refiner-reported, 2018-2021) x the Russian share of the refiner's crude (China and India: Comtrade crude imports from Russia / world in tonnes; Turkey: Russian crude, Russian-reported exports and CREA 2021, / 31 Mt as in energy.json; UAE: Russian product imports / product exports) x the same calibration 0.53/0.699/1.0. Units and stage are the same as energy.json laundered_oil (EUR bn product value, before hub pass-on, crude-content factor, EU x0.62 and GDP cap), so the builder must apply the same steps to the base. Russian shares 2018-2021: China 15.5% every year; India 1.0-2.1%; Turkey 9-26% (2019 peak when Iran's waivers ended); UAE 0.3-2.1%. Pre-war total (central): EUR 3.8bn (2018), 5.2 (2019), 2.9 (2020), 4.5 (2021); China 2.4-3.7bn a year, India 0.2-0.7, Turkey 0.2-1.2, UAE <0.1. Post-war central: 16-30bn a year, so most of the rise is India (EUR 0.4bn pre-war vs 8-20bn). For buyers mainly supplied by China (Hong Kong, Singapore, Philippines, Panama, Australia, Korea, Malaysia) the pre-war base is large: Hong Kong 0.51 vs 0.91 in 2023, Singapore 0.73 vs 2.60. base_2018_2021 is the nominal 2018-2021 mean; base_2018_2021_at_2019_2021_prices revalues volumes at each refiner's 2019-2021 export unit value (use it if the map compares at constant prices). g: log-linear 2018-2021 slope of the constant-price series, shrunk 70% toward the pooled slope (+5.8%/yr), capped at +-10%/yr; low/high = central -+ max(5 points, half the distance to the own slope), always including zero. Recommend the same 3-year half-life damping as trend.json when extending g to 2022-2026.

notes: Scripts: working/round4a/round4a.py (model) and working/round4a/assemble.py (this file); downloads in working/round4a/raw/. Weakest assumptions: (1) the 2018-2020 company tax history uses macro indices, not company data (no KSE back-data exists); (2) China's exporter factor 0.75 (0.45-1.10) for the Russian share in export-quota refineries is a judgement; (3) China's 2025 and 2026 refinery runs and 2026 product exports are estimates from monthly press data; (4) EU refinery export shares are rounded ranges, not refinery-level data; (5) pre-war growth rates rest on four noisy years and are shrunk hard toward the pooled trend.
